7: Canaanites who have fallen into a pit or a place of danger — the observer is not obligated to raise them up, etc. In Chapter “Eilu Metziot” (26a), Rav Yosef thought to say that the teaching that states, “Canaanites and shepherds of small livestock, we do not raise them nor lower them,” allows for raising them in exchange for payment, due to the concern for hostility. Abaye said to him: He could say, "My son is on the roof," (Rashi explains: if I do not lower him, he will die, and I prefer to forgo my wages to save him). Or, "I have an appointment with the governor," (Rashi explains: the official set a time for me, and if I do not go, my profit will turn into a loss). The halacha follows Abaye. Similarly, Rav Yosef thought to say that delivering a gentile baby on Shabbat for pay is allowed to prevent hostility. Abaye countered: He could say, "We have Shabbat laws to observe," etc.

Rav Yosef also thought to say that assisting for payment is permitted to avoid hostility. Abaye objected, saying he could explain, "If she is single," etc. In all these cases, the halacha follows Abaye, as seen above in Siman 154, and as implied by the Talmud’s language: "Rav Yosef thought to say," meaning this was an initial assumption until Abaye challenged him and he retracted his original understanding.

Regarding the phrase "or a place of danger," it seems that our teacher (the author) holds that the rule of not raising them applies to someone who falls into a pit with water — a life-threatening situation where immediate rescue is necessary to prevent drowning. That is why he added "or a place of danger," implying that even the mention of falling into a pit refers to a dangerous situation.
Rambam explained this more explicitly in Laws of Murder, Chapter 4:

"A gentile with whom we are not at war, and Jewish shepherds of small livestock, or similar individuals — we do not cause their death, but it is forbidden to save them if they are dying. For example, if one saw such a person fall into the sea, they should not pull him out," etc.

Thus, Rambam clarified that the rule of "not raising them" applies when the person is near death, such as falling into the sea. This is also the view of the Tosafot in Avodah Zarah (20a) who questioned the position permitting giving gifts to gentiles, based on a verse. They resolved that the verse refers to a gift that does not sustain their life, since even without the gift, they would not die — unlike pulling someone from a pit, which saves them from near-certain death, raising concerns of sustaining gentile progeny.

Rambam’s wording, "a gentile with whom we are not at war," instead of simply "a gentile," seems intended to reconcile the Tosafot’s difficulty with the teaching, "we do not lower them," since in Massechet Sofrim it states, "The most righteous of the gentiles should be killed." The Jerusalem Talmud explains that this applies during wartime. It seems that Rambam wrote this phrase to align with that interpretation.
